U.S. rail traffic rose 7.3% in the week ending November 14, 2026, compared with the same week last year, as double-digit intermodal growth outpaced gains in conventional carload shipments, according to the Association of American Railroads .
Intermodal volume increased 10.7% year over year, while total carloads rose 3.3%, AAR said in a weekly update. Eight of the 10 carload commodity groups recorded gains.
(Chart: AAR)
Motor vehicles and parts posted the strongest percentage increase among carload categories, rising 16.2%. Forest products followed with a 14% gain, while metallic ores and metals increased 10.7% and petroleum and petroleum products advanced 10.3%.
The remaining categories posting increases were farm products excluding grain, and food, up 3.1%; chemicals, up 2.3%; nonmetallic minerals, up 2.1%; and coal, up 0.9%. Grain shipments fell 4.7%.
Year-to-date traffic advances 4%
Through the first 45 weeks of 2026, total U.S. rail traffic increased 4% compared with the corresponding period in 2025. Intermodal volume rose 5%, while carload traffic gained 2.7%.
Grain remained the strongest year-to-date carload category, up 9.4%, despite its weekly decline. Metallic ores and metals increased 8.8%, and petroleum and petroleum products rose 7.8%. Coal was the only carload category below its year-earlier level for the year to date, down 1.5%.
North American rail traffic also rises
Across nine reporting U.S., Canadian and Mexican railroads, combined weekly traffic increased 7.2% year over year. North American carloads rose 3.7%, while intermodal volume climbed 10.5%. Total traffic for the first 45 weeks of the year increased 3.5%.
Why it matters: The results show rail traffic growth extending across most major commodity groups, while forest products and automotive bucked high interest rates that have held down home construction and car sales for much of the year.
